---
title: "lmd: Markdown and Lua in the same file"
description: "Write Lua cells whose results are markdown, and markdown fragments that are Lua values: read metadata and compute on it, repeat markup over a list, share state between cells, and build reusable fragments, all inside the document."
# Sample values read by the live cells on this page; see "Reaching for metadata".
version: 12.1
team: [ada, grace, linus]
---

An **lmd** cell (Lua and markdown) is an executable cell whose language is
Lua and whose result is markdown. It needs no engine or runtime: Quarto runs
it while rendering, and whatever the cell returns takes the cell's place in
the document. Two ideas, layered, make it more than "Lua in a code block":

1. **Markdown in your Lua.** Inside the cell, a piece of markdown is an
   expression. `{=: … :=}` is a block value and `{=[ … ]=}` an inline value,
   written as markdown and handed to you as the `pandoc.Blocks` or
   `pandoc.Inlines` you would otherwise assemble out of constructors. Inside
   such a fragment, `` `{lmd} expr` `` puts a Lua value back into the
   markdown, so the two languages nest in both directions.
2. **Lua in your markdown.** A ```` ```{lmd} ```` block is replaced by what it
   returns, where it sits; `` `{lmd} expr` `` in a paragraph is replaced by the
   value of the expression. A cell is a filter that acts in place, so it
   never has to name a class to match on.

A [Lua filter](lua-filters.qmd) is Lua *for* your markdown: a separate file,
applied to the whole document from outside. lmd is markdown right in your
Lua, and Lua right in your markdown, in the same file.

@demo-first-cell is the whole thing in one cell:

::::: {#demo-first-cell .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/01-first-cell/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "A first lmd cell"
stuff: [a, b, c, d]
---

The front matter of this document has `stuff: [a, b, c, d]`. The cell below
produces one bold paragraph per item:

```{lmd}
return meta.stuff:map(function(v) return {=: **`{lmd} v`** :=} end)
```
````

One cell, four paragraphs. `meta.stuff` is the front-matter list; `:map` is a `pandoc.List` method; `{=: … :=}` turns markdown into a value; the inner `` `{lmd} v` `` puts each item back into the markdown; the list of blocks the cell returns replaces the cell. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/01-first-cell)
:::::

Everything on this page is a pattern of use. The mechanics are introduced as
each pattern needs them and collected in [The rules, in one place](#the-rules-in-one-place)
near the end.

Two facts shape all of it. All the cells of a document run in **one Lua
state, in document order**, so a cell can define something a later cell
uses. And cells run **after the engines and before everything else**: user
filters, shortcodes, cross-references and callouts all see what a cell
returned, exactly as if you had typed it.

## Reaching for metadata

The most common reason to reach for a cell is a value in the front matter.
This page's own front matter has:

```yaml
version: 12.1
team: [ada, grace, linus]
```

and the cells on this page read it. `meta` is the document metadata as a
Lua value you navigate: `meta.version`, `meta.team[1]`, `meta.author.name`
for nested keys. Each metadata value arrives in the shape a Lua filter would
see it:

| front-matter value | in Lua |
|---|---|
| a string (markdown by default) | `Inlines`, so emphasis and code in a title survive |
| a number, a boolean | the number, the boolean |
| a list | a `pandoc.List`, with `#`, `ipairs`, `:map`, `:filter` |
| a map | a value you keep navigating, `meta.author.affil` |

A path that may be absent is read with `quarto.metadata.get("a.b.c")`,
which returns `nil` for a missing key where `meta.a.b.c` would raise. The
two agree everywhere else; numeric segments index lists, so
`quarto.metadata.get("authors.2.name")` is `meta.authors[2].name`.

### Computing on it

The `{{{< meta version >}}}` shortcode inserts a value. A cell can also
*compute* on it. Live, from this page's front matter:

````markdown
The team has `{lmd} #meta.team` members:
`{lmd} table.concat(meta.team:map(pandoc.utils.stringify), ", ")`.
The lead is `{lmd} pandoc.utils.stringify(meta.team[1]):upper()`,
and this is version `{lmd} meta.version`.
````

> The team has `{lmd} #meta.team` members:
> `{lmd} table.concat(meta.team:map(pandoc.utils.stringify), ", ")`.
> The lead is `{lmd} pandoc.utils.stringify(meta.team[1]):upper()`,
> and this is version `{lmd} meta.version`.

Two things to know, both visible above:

- A **number or boolean** reads the way `tostring` prints it: `12.1`, `3`,
  `true`. That courtesy is the inline cell's own. A `pandoc` constructor
  takes Inlines and strings, as in pandoc, so `pandoc.Strong(meta.version)`
  wants `tostring()`, and so does an inline cell *inside a fragment*, which
  is spliced into the constructor call the fragment becomes (the
  [lists](#repeating-markdown-over-a-list) below show one).
- Metadata **strings are `Inlines`**, not Lua strings, so `table.concat` and
  `:upper()` need `pandoc.utils.stringify` first. Leave the `Inlines` alone
  when the formatting should survive: `` `{lmd} meta.title` `` renders a
  title's emphasis and code as written.

@demo-metadata puts the two halves together with a nested key and a
fallback for a key that is not there:

::::: {#demo-metadata .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/02-metadata/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "Reading metadata"
version: 12.1
team: [ada, grace, linus]
author:
  name: Ada
  affil: Analytical Engines
---

The team has `{lmd} #meta.team` members:
`{lmd} table.concat(meta.team:map(pandoc.utils.stringify), ", ")`.
The lead is `{lmd} pandoc.utils.stringify(meta.team[1]):upper()`.

This is version `{lmd} meta.version` (a number in the front matter; an
inline cell writes it the way `tostring` would).

`{lmd} meta.author.name` works at `{lmd} quarto.metadata.get("author.affil")`.
A key that may be absent is read with `quarto.metadata.get`, which returns
`nil` instead of raising: `{lmd} quarto.metadata.get("author.phone") or "no phone on file"`.
````

Reading and computing on metadata: a count, a joined list, a string method, a number written as `tostring` would print it, a nested key through `meta` and through `quarto.metadata.get`, and a fallback for an absent key. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/02-metadata)
:::::

## Repeating markdown over a list

The second pattern: the same markup for every element of a list. The
natural shape is `:map` from the list to a fragment per element, and then
the question is what to do with the pieces.

**Items of a list.** The item of a `pandoc.BulletList` is a list of blocks.
An inline fragment wrapped in `pandoc.Plain` gives a tight list; a block
fragment gives an item of one or more paragraphs:

````markdown
```{lmd}
return pandoc.BulletList(meta.authors:map(function(a)
  return pandoc.Plain({=[ `{lmd} a.name` (`{lmd} a.role`) ]=})
end))
```
````

Two shapes look right and are not. An inline fragment passed *bare* as an
item, `return {=[ … ]=}` inside the `:map`, is coerced one inline at a time,
and the item renders one word per line. And one `{=: - item :=}` fragment
per element gives a list of one-item lists, rendered as separate lists.

**A section per element.** Accumulate into a `pandoc.Blocks` with `:extend`,
and return it:

````markdown
```{lmd}
local out = pandoc.Blocks({})
for i, t in ipairs(meta.team) do
  out:extend({=:
### `{lmd} t`

Member number `{lmd} tostring(i)`.
:=})
end
return out
```
````

Headings built this way get their ids from their final text, unique across
the document, so they are linkable and show up in the table of contents like
any other heading. The `tostring(i)` is needed here: an inline cell inside
a fragment is spliced into the `pandoc.Para` call the paragraph becomes,
and constructors take Inlines and strings, not numbers.

**Two fragments.** `a .. b` concatenates two `Blocks` values, for the case
where a loop is more than you need.

@demo-lists shows all of these, and an ordered list:

::::: {#demo-lists .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/03-lists/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "Repeating markdown over a list"
team: [ada, grace, linus]
authors:
  - name: Ada
    role: lead
  - name: Grace
    role: reviewer
---

## A tight list

Each item of a bullet list is a list of blocks, so an inline fragment is
wrapped in `pandoc.Plain`:

```{lmd}
return pandoc.BulletList(meta.authors:map(function(a)
  return pandoc.Plain({=[ `{lmd} a.name` (`{lmd} a.role`) ]=})
end))
```

## Items with several blocks

A block fragment can hold any number of blocks, so an item can be more
than one paragraph:

```{lmd}
return pandoc.BulletList(meta.authors:map(function(a)
  return {=:
`{lmd} a.name` is the `{lmd} a.role`.

A second paragraph about `{lmd} a.name`.
:=}
end))
```

## An ordered list

```{lmd}
return pandoc.OrderedList(meta.authors:map(function(a)
  return pandoc.Plain({=[ `{lmd} a.name` ]=})
end))
```

## A section per item

```{lmd}
local out = pandoc.Blocks({})
for i, t in ipairs(meta.team) do
  out:extend({=:
### `{lmd} t`

Member number `{lmd} tostring(i)`.
:=})
end
return out
```
````

A tight list from `pandoc.Plain` items, items with several blocks from block fragments, an ordered list, and a section per element from `:extend`. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/03-lists)
:::::

## Setup cells and shared state

A cell with no `return` leaves nothing in the document. That makes it the
natural place for definitions: every cell of a document runs in the same Lua
state, in document order, so a variable or function defined in one cell is
there for every cell after it, block and inline alike.

::::: {#demo-shared-state .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/04-shared-state/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "Setup cells and shared state"
---

A cell with no `return` leaves nothing behind. Everything it defines is
visible to the cells after it:

```{lmd}
greeting = "Hello"
function badge(text)
  return {=[ [`{lmd} text`]{.badge .text-bg-secondary} ]=}
end
```

## `{lmd} greeting`, world

A `{lmd} badge("new")` feature and a `{lmd} badge("beta")` one. The heading
above got its id from its final text.
````

A setup cell defines `greeting` and `badge`; the heading and the paragraph after it use them. The heading's id is `hello-world`, derived from its final text. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/04-shared-state)
:::::

Document order runs top to bottom through nested blocks: a cell inside a
fenced div runs before a top-level cell that follows the div, and an inline
cell in the paragraph *above* a setup cell sees `nil` for what that cell
defines.

## Fragments as functions

A function that returns a fragment is a reusable piece of markup, with the
arguments spliced in wherever an inline `` `{lmd} expr` `` appears. A fragment can also
hold a block cell of its own, which is how a function splices a whole body
of blocks into its markup:

::::: {#demo-fragment-functions .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/05-fragment-functions/document.html"}
`````markdown
---
title: "Fragments as functions"
---

A function that returns a fragment is a reusable piece of markup. The
fragment here contains a block cell of its own, which splices `body` in,
so the outer cell needs a four-backtick fence:

````{lmd}
local function card(title, body)
  return {=:
::: {.card .p-3 .mb-3}
### `{lmd} title`

```{lmd}
return body
```
:::
:=}
end
return card("Hello", {=: Some *body* text. :=}) .. card("Bye", {=: More. :=})
````
`````

`card(title, body)` returns a fragment whose heading splices `title` inline and whose nested block cell splices `body`. The outer cell uses four backticks because it contains a three-backtick fence, the ordinary markdown rule. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/05-fragment-functions)
:::::

Two markdown nesting rules come up here. A cell that contains a fenced block
needs a longer fence than the one inside it. And an inline cell whose
fragment holds a code span needs double-backtick delimiters, since single
backticks pair up left to right.

## Conditional content

A cell that returns `nil` vanishes, so an `if` around the `return` is all it
takes to include something conditionally:

::::: {#demo-conditional .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/06-conditional/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "Conditional content"
draft: true
version: 0.4
---

A cell that returns `nil` vanishes, so a condition around `return` is all
it takes:

```{lmd}
if meta.draft then
  return {=:
::: {.callout-warning}
This is a draft of version `{lmd} tostring(meta.version)`.
:::
:=}
end
```

The same works per format:

```{lmd}
if quarto.doc.is_format("html") then
  return {=: You are reading the HTML version. :=}
end
return {=: You are not reading the HTML version. :=}
```
````

A callout that appears only because `draft: true` is in the front matter, and a branch on `quarto.doc.is_format`. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/06-conditional)
:::::

The callout renders as a callout because whatever a cell returns is
processed as if typed: fenced divs with classes, cross-reference labels and
callouts inside a fragment all work.

## A filter on a piece of markdown

A fragment is a `pandoc.Blocks` value, and `Blocks` has `walk`. So the
filter vocabulary you may know from [Lua filters](lua-filters.qmd) applies to a
value in hand rather than to the whole document:

::::: {#demo-walk .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/07-walk/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "A filter on a piece of markdown"
---

A fragment is a `pandoc.Blocks` value, so it has `walk`:

```{lmd}
local frag = {=: Some *text* to shout. :=}
return frag:walk({ Str = function(s) return pandoc.Str(s.text:upper()) end })
```
````

`walk` with a `Str` handler over a fragment: a one-off filter on one piece of markdown. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/07-walk)
:::::

Every `pandoc.*` constructor is available too, for whatever is easier to
build from data than to write out (a `pandoc.Span` with computed attributes,
for instance). The Lua filters page describes the API.

## Seeing what ran, and when a cell fails

`--| echo: true` at the top of a block cell keeps the Lua the cell actually
ran visible above its result. Fragments appear rewritten into `pandoc`
constructor calls, which is also the clearest explanation of what a
fragment *is*:

::::: {#demo-echo .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/lmd/08-echo/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "Seeing what ran"
---

With `--| echo: true` the cell shows the Lua it ran, fragments rewritten
into `pandoc` constructor calls, above its result:

```{lmd}
--| echo: true
return {=: A paragraph with *emphasis*, built from a fragment. :=}
```
````

The desugared Lua above the result. `--|` is the option syntax for lmd cells, as `#|` is for Python and R cells. [View source](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/tree/main/examples/lmd/08-echo)
:::::

A cell that fails produces an error located at the failing line, with the
cell left displayed as a code block so the page still renders and the code
can be read:

```
Error: [Q-26-4] lmd cell failed
    ╭─[ report.qmd:32:1 ]
    │
 32 │ error("boom")
    │ ──────┬──────
    │       ╰──────── runtime error: report.qmd:32: boom
stack traceback:
	[C]: in function 'error'
	report.qmd:32: in main chunk
────╯
```

The failures, each with a reference page: the Lua does not parse
([`Q-26-1`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-1.qmd)); a fragment holds markdown that
cannot be built, such as a footnote or a shortcode
([`Q-26-2`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-2.qmd)); an inline fragment parses to more
than one block ([`Q-26-3`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-3.qmd)); the Lua raises at
run time ([`Q-26-4`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-4.qmd)); a block cell returns
something that is not blocks ([`Q-26-5`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-5.qmd)); an
inline cell produces something that is not inlines
([`Q-26-6`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-6.qmd)); the cell options do not parse
([`Q-26-7`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-7.qmd)). A markdown syntax error inside a
fragment is reported with the markdown reader's own code and underlined
inside the fragment. The [error reference](../../errors/index.qmd) lists
them all.

### Writing about lmd

This page shows cells without running them, which is the ordinary markdown
rule described under [Computations](computations.qmd#displaying-code-cells-without-running-them):
a cell inside a `markdown` fence with more backticks is displayed. In prose,
`` `{lmd}` `` on its own is a mention and stays as code; a tag followed by
an expression runs.

## The rules, in one place

**What a cell may return.** A block cell returns a Block, a list of Blocks
(a `pandoc.Blocks`, a plain table of blocks, or a list of such lists), or
`nil`. An inline cell evaluates to an Inline, a list of Inlines, a string, a
number, a boolean, or `nil`; a string is split into words and spaces as
pandoc does, and a number or boolean is written as `tostring` prints it.

**The three fragment forms.**

| form | value | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `{=: … :=}` | `pandoc.Blocks` | any markdown; a top-level paragraph is a `Para` |
| `{=[ … ]=}` | `pandoc.Inlines` | one paragraph or nothing, else [`Q-26-3`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-3.qmd) |
| `{= … =}` | `pandoc.Nodes` | decided by context: blocks where blocks go (a paragraph stays a paragraph), inlines where inlines go (a one-paragraph fragment unwraps) |

The two marked forms cover everything on this page. The unmarked form exists
for a value that is passed to both kinds of position; `pandoc.Para({= x =})`
and `pandoc.Div({= x =})` both work.

**When cells run.** After the engines, so a Python or R cell has already run
and neither side sees the other's variables; before user filters,
shortcodes, cross-references, callouts and the table of contents. One Lua
state per document; cells run in document order, pre-order through nested
blocks.

**Heading ids** follow the final text of the heading, after every cell has
run, and are unique across the document. An explicit `{#id}` is kept.

**What a cell can use.** The `pandoc` and `quarto` tables a Lua filter gets
(constructors, `pandoc.utils`, `quarto.doc.is_format`, `quarto.utils`),
`meta` and `quarto.metadata.get`, `FORMAT`, and `require` for a `.lua` file
next to the document.

## Current limitations

- **Footnotes inside a fragment** fail the cell
  ([`Q-26-2`](../../errors/lmd/Q-26-2.qmd)). Put the note in the document
  body.
- **Shortcodes inside a fragment** fail the cell. Read the value in Lua
  instead: `` `{lmd} meta.key` `` rather than `{{{< meta key >}}}`.
- **Inline cells in attribute values** (a fenced div's `data-x="…"`, a link
  title) are not evaluated.
- **Numbers inside a fragment.** A top-level inline cell writes a number or
  boolean as `tostring` would. One inside a fragment is spliced into a
  `pandoc` constructor argument, which takes only Inlines and strings, so
  there it is still `` `{lmd} tostring(i)` ``.
- **Modules.** `require` of a `.lua` file next to the document works; a
  module written in lmd (a `.lmd` file with fragments) does not load yet.
  Reusable lmd modules are coming.

## Where this leads

A listing declared with `type: metadata` renders nothing of its own and
publishes its resolved items at `meta.listings.<id>`, for a cell to turn into
whatever markup the page wants; see [Listings as data](../projects/listings.qmd#listings-as-data).
And a cell can hand what it builds to a React component with
`quarto.component`, so the markup it writes is the no-script version of an
interactive element; see [Building the element from Lua](components.qmd#building-the-element-from-lua).
The `websites/09-interactive-listing` example in the repository has both
together.
